3d_ai.title: KeyShot 2026 review: fast, easy 3D rendering and with AI tools you might actually use
3d_ai.summary_original: AI Shots brings generative AI into the heart of the rendering workflow.
3d_ai.content_original:
Our Verdict
KeyShot 2026 represents another significant milestone of development for the popular product visualisation tool. They continue to embrace AI to improve rendered output and simplify workflows. This doesn't take away from the user's ability to harness their creativity to produce some truly impressive rendered results. The software is easier to use than ever, and it's faster too.
For
- Simple and intuitive
- AI tools you might actually use
- New render output tools
Against
- Expensive
- Still only for product visualisation
Why you can trust Creative Bloq
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Having used the best rendering software for over two decades, one of my favourites is KeyShot Studio. Despite not being my go-to choice for rendering most architectural scenes, if I'm ever rendering smaller scenes or individual products, then I know there's hardly anything better on the market.
Now at version 2026, KeyShot is stronger than ever with a slew of new features to improve the user experience and elevate its capabilities. These include more realistic AI output through AI Shots with the ability to now edit and upscale, an upgraded Move Tool + Custom Pivot, and an all-new gallery feature.
It wouldn't be a software upgrade without some mention of AI, would it? In fact, KeyShot has been using AI for many years, specifically to deliver progressive denoising. But as for AI features, the primary one is AI Shots, which was introduced partway through the 2025 software cycle. KeyShot has determined this is the way to go, devoting a significant amount of development time to improving it.
If you're looking for help on where to start, then you could follow my KeyShot and Photoshop advice for perfect renders every time as well as find out how to create cinematic cameras in KeyShot. To complement KeyShot, you will also need one of the best 3D software packages.
KeyShot 2026: plans and pricing
• KeyShot Professional for $108.25 per month (billed annually) 
• KeyShot Business provides seat management features
Most Creative Bloq readers will need a KeyShot Professional subscription. This provides the complete 3D visualisation toolkit for individual designers, freelancers, and small studios. This costs $108.25 per month, although it's billed annually at $1,299.
If you do happen to be a larger team requiring centralised seat management, then you'll have to upgrade to KeyShot Business. For the privilege, this costs $133.25 per month, which equates to $1,599 billed annually.
Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.
Value score: 4/5
KeyShot 2026: features
• AI Shots brings generative AI into the heart of the rendering workflow
• A new Gallery window makes it easier to find and organise renderings
The single biggest feature improvement in 2026 is AI Shots. This is KeyShot's generative AI workflow, and it was introduced in KeyShot 2025.2. With it you can either generate images from a CAD model or edit an existing image. Either way, it means artists can utilise generative AI in a dedicated 3D rendering tool rather than relying on alternative tools that were not designed with 3D in mind.
The AI Shots tool is particularly useful for artists wanting to create multiple images with small variations. They can do that easily using the generate multiple images feature when entering the prompt. KeyShot has also improved the overall AI model so it now works with much shorter prompts compared to version 2025.
One of the best improvements of AI Shots is the upscaling feature that enables artists to double or quadruple the resolution of both traditional 3D renderings and AI Shots in a "fraction of the time". This proves more effective than generating an AI shot at a lower resolution and then upscaling.
Beyond AI shots, KeyShot includes a more powerful Custom Pivot + Move Tool. With it users can "give parts or groups multiple custom pivots in addition to origin and centre. These custom pivots can be named for organisational purposes and are stored in your scene."
The move tool gizmo has now also been synchronised between realtime and geometry views, which makes it much more straight forward to work in both views at the same time. It was previously a little confusing, and even though this is only a user experience improvement, it's still a meaningful one.
The final feature to mention is called Gallery, and I love it. It's a new window, and it lets you quickly and easily find your render output once your renderings are complete. It's much more than just a viewer, though. With it you can search, sort, and organise all your rendered output.
Features score: 4.5/5
KeyShot 2026: user interface and experience
• Creating product visualisations in KeyShot is an absolute breeze
• The new AI shots feature provides a generative tool for customising the results
KeyShot is a wonderful piece of visualisation software that takes hardly any time at all to get your head around. Materials, lighting, camera, and environment tools are clearly laid out and easily accessible through various panels and menus. I had no issues finding settings quickly, and with results instantly displayed in the real-time view, it's easy to tweak settings until you get a result you're happy with.
I love how easy it is to cycle through lighting setups and see immediately whether your model catches the reflections nicely or not. With plenty of lighting and material options in the local and cloud libraries artists can quickly translate their 3D model into a beautiful photorealistic visual. Beyond setting up the scene it's also effortless to add post-effects including denoising, sharpening, and bloom, amongst many others.
AI Shots offers a basic interface for adjusting your output using a short prompt. Before doing so, though, you'll have to download near 20GB of AI data, so make sure you've got the necessary storage space before deciding whether KeyShot along with its AI tool is the right visualisation product for you.
I tested AI Shots on my MacBook Pro with 16GB RAM. This is less than the recommended 32GB RAM, but with RAM prices showing no signs of slowing down, I think my laptop is a fair representation of what a lot of users will have access to.
During my tests I found that all elements of the tool, including image generation, upscaling, and element replacement, worked without a hitch. It never crashed, and the progress bar kept moving in the right direction. My only issue with it is that it is quite slow, with some prompts taking upwards of five minutes to process. I found it to be a helpful tool, but it was subject to misinterpreting some of my prompts and couldn't therefore be relied upon for perfect recreation of prompts.
User Experience score: 4.5/5
KeyShot 2026: who is it for?
• KeyShot is designed almost exclusively for product visualisation
KeyShot was built with product visualisation in mind. It offers a simple workflow for 3D artists who regularly find themselves visualising products or product designers who want an in-house solution for creating their own images. KeyShot will work for other types of scenes, but if you're working in film, games, or architecture, then you'll need a dedicated rendering engine such as V-Ray or Cycles (Blender).
Buy it if...
- You create visualisations from CAD
- You need to do this quickly and accurately
- You want a simple rendering solution for small to medium 3D scenes
Don't buy it if...
- You work in film, games, or architecture
- You're regularly rendering large scenes
- You need a rendering engine plugin for your favourite 3D software

3d_ai.title: AIに「法隆寺の五重塔」を作らせてみた　修正を重ねてたどり着いた驚きの完成度
3d_ai.summary_original: Dotsで法隆寺の五重塔を3D化し、UE5で動かすまでを紹介。専門家の指摘や論文を基に修正を重ね、AIによる制作の可能性と、建築物の構造を理解して精度を確保する難しさ、専門家による監修の必要性を実感した。
3d_ai.content_original:
9月29日に、OpenAIがChatGPT向けの新機能「Dots」を発表しました。AIエージェントが常駐し、仕事をお願いすると、必要に応じてGPTのスレッドを立ち上げて制御し、完遂するまで作業してくれます。メール確認や送付、スケジュールチェック、請求書の作成など、事務仕事に使えますが、クリエイティブ分野でも使えることがわかってきました。例えば、ユーザーには仮想のコンピュータが割り当てられるのですが、そのなかに3Dツールの「Blender」が含まれており、ローカルPCがなくても、指示を続けるだけで、3Dモデリングを行ってくれるのです。そこで、法隆寺の五重塔を作らせてみて、どこまで品質を高められるのかを試してみました。
複数のAIを指揮する「Dots」。2日がかりで五重塔の3Dモデルを作ってみた
筆者がDotsに作らせたのは、奈良の法隆寺にある、国宝の五重塔です。7世紀末に建てられたと推定されており、現存する木造五重塔としては世界最古であり、高さは32.55mもあります。ほんの軽い気持ちで作り始めたのですが、断続的な作業に２日あまりを費やし、かなり迫力のある3Dモデルを作り出すことができました。
これまで、ChatGPTを利用する際には面倒なことがありました。タスクごとにスレッドを分けないと、コンテキストが混じるためにうまく機能しないことです。ところが多数のタスクを扱うと検索性が落ちるため、どこに何があるのかがわからなくなってきます。
その点Dotsは、タスク内容に応じて別のスレッドを立て、そこにプロンプトを送って指示し、作業を進めてくれます。思いついたタスクを次々に指示しても、仕事内容に応じて、タスクをいくつにも分けてくれます。GPTで動かしている作業全体を統括して、他のAIエージェントをオーケストレーションする仕組みになっています。
現在は、個人向けには100ドル以上のProの各プランのユーザーに提供されています。Dotsについては「使える」「使えない」と、X上でかなり意見が分かれているようです。筆者は実際に使ってみて、「めちゃくちゃ使える」と判断しました。

3d_ai.title: How to Build an Atmospheric Stylized Lighthouse Scene with a Custom Modular Set
3d_ai.summary_original: Albert Serrano explained how he created tileable materials for the scene, shared his tips on ensuring smooth blending between different materials, and talked about how he made an atlas of hand-sculpted plants to create stylized vegetation.
3d_ai.content_original:
How to Build an Atmospheric Stylized Lighthouse Scene with a Custom Modular Set
Albert Serrano explained how he created tileable materials for the scene, shared his tips on ensuring smooth blending between different materials, and talked about how he made an atlas of hand-sculpted plants to create stylized vegetation.
Introduction
My name is Albert Serrano, and I am a 3D Environment Artist currently working at MercurySteam in Madrid, Spain. I have always been passionate about video games, and over time, that passion grew into curiosity about how they were actually made. This eventually led me to explore the world of 3D art and discover that creating the environments I admired in games could become a career.
I started learning Blender in my spare time while studying Audiovisual Media at the university. Later, I continued my studies in Valencia while also developing my 3D skills independently, aiming to build a strong portfolio and break into the video game industry.
I have now been working at MercurySteam for over three years, and I am proud to have had the opportunity to contribute to a prestigious title for Nintendo.
I have always been drawn to stylized art and the unique visual language it brings to games. Overwatch, World of Warcraft, and Sea of Thieves are some of my biggest inspirations, especially for their strong shapes, attractive colors, and distinctive environments. These influences have naturally shaped my own approach and the kind of worlds I enjoy creating.
Lighthouse: the Concept
I had gone some time without working on a personal project when I came across this concept by Gustav Nordgren. I immediately loved it and felt it was a great excuse to get back to creating. I gathered references for the visual style and began planning the materials and assets, especially the water, which I considered the key element in achieving the overall look of the scene.
Blocking Out
I started by creating a simple blockout in Blender and bringing it into Unreal Engine. This helped me establish the proportions, camera distance, and overall composition, while giving me a clear idea of the key elements I needed to focus on for the final scene.
Materials
At this stage, I identified the elements that could rely on tileable materials, since they would be repeated throughout the scene. I then started developing these materials and trims in Substance 3D Designer, using them to define the stylized look I wanted for the scene.
I also created a modular set of wooden pieces in different sizes, sculpting them in ZBrush and giving them enough texel density to be easily reused and scaled throughout the scene, as they would be applied in many different ways across the environment.
Water
For the water, I wanted something stylized yet lightweight enough to keep the scene running smoothly in Unreal Engine. Since at that point I didn't have enough experience with Unreal Engine's Material Editor to create something this complex from scratch, I followed a tutorial by Ghislain Girardot and made a few small adjustments so that it would fit the look of the scene. The amount of variation you can create by tweaking a few parameters made this one of my favorite parts of the project.
Props
For the props, I worked mainly in ZBrush, shaping them to match the stylized look I wanted. This is always one of the more enjoyable parts of the process, as it gives me more time to focus on individual assets and add personality to them. I wanted to keep them fairly simple overall, while still giving them enough detail to feel interesting and relevant to the scene.
Vegetation
For vegetation, I created a simple atlas containing the different types of plants I needed in ZBrush and then textured it in Substance 3D Painter. I also added a few parameters in Unreal Engine to adjust their colors directly in the engine, allowing me to easily create variations and adjust them to fit the scene.
Modules
Once the main scene looked fairly solid, I decided to explore a second camera angle and expand the environment. I already had most of the necessary assets and materials, so adding a few simple modular elements felt like a good way to give the project more depth without significantly increasing the workload. Since I could reuse the tileable materials I had already created, I was able to build the new area relatively quickly.
Small Tip
To better blend the different wall materials, I used the same plaster material with a different tint through an additional Vertex Color channel. This added an extra layer between the plaster and stone, helping the materials blend together more naturally and allowing me to paint it in other areas to add more variation to the walls. It also made it possible for me to control the darkness of the tint.
Decals
Another small detail that made a big difference was the use of bird-dropping decals, which I created in Photoshop. They might seem insignificant, but they helped give the scene the character I was looking for and added more variation to the environment.
Making the Scene Feel Alive
One of the things I value most when looking at an environment is the feeling that the world is alive. I think these small touches give a scene character and greatly enhance the atmosphere it conveys. With that in mind, I added a couple of particle systems for the fish underwater, the seagulls, and the subtle wind lines, along with movement in the water and seaweed, and set up a camera shot designed to bring everything together.
Finishing Touches
For the final touches, I adjusted several post-processing settings to bring out the colours and saturation, as I wanted the scene to have a distinctive, colourful look with slightly stronger contrast in certain areas. I also refined the lighting, using a Directional Light as the main light source, which I kept close to the original concept from the beginning, as I felt it suited the scene perfectly. I added a few Point Lights in specific areas to create more visual interest, and finally introduced water caustics to enhance the underwater atmosphere and complete the look.
Advice for Beginners
I still feel like I have a lot to learn, especially after only a few years in the industry, but one thing I would encourage any beginner artist to do is to start projects and commit to finishing them. I'm not saying you have to commit 100% to every project you start, since we all have unfinished projects, but it definitely helps to take some of them seriously and push yourself to see them through to the end, until you can look back at the result and feel happy with what you have achieved.
Sometimes you reach a point where you look at your work and feel that something is not working, and it can be very frustrating. It is easy to lose motivation and move on to something else, but learning to work through those moments is an important part of the process. By continuing to work on the piece and figuring out how to solve the problems you are not happy with, you will gradually improve. In my opinion, the process is ultimately more important than the final result, as the finished piece is simply the outcome of everything you have learned and worked through along the way.

ai_agent.title: 17 tech executives reveal how AI agents are changing work and hiring
ai_agent.summary_original: Tech leaders from Zoom, Figma, ServiceNow, and more reveal how AI agents are reshaping work, hiring, and the software business.
ai_agent.content_original:
This week, AI Insider hosted a dinner, sponsored by Dash0, in San Francisco for tech executives. I started with a simple question.
"Who had an AI agent help them at work today?"
Every hand went up.
Then I asked a follow-up.
"Who had more than five AI agents helping them at work today?"
Again, every hand stayed in the air.
Around the table were Zoom CTO XD Huang; Figma VP of Engineering Josh Clemm; Coursera CTO Mustafa Furniturewala; ServiceNow executive Ashraf Karim; Glean CTO T.R. "Vish" Vishwanath; Netlify CEO Matt Biilmann; PagerDuty engineering leader Manu Gurudatha; Yahoo Mail GM Kyle Miller; Lime CTO Jon Jenkins; Proofpoint AI security chief Ravi Ithal; Temporal cofounder and CTO Maxim Fateev; Inworld CEO Kylan Gibbs; Xero engineering leader Diya Jolly; MinIO CTO Ugur Tigli; Tribe AI partner Pooja Brown; Basis cofounder Creston Brooks; and Empirik CEO Kartik Chandrayana.
No one debated whether AI will kill us. These are experienced tech leaders from the trenches wrestling with real questions, such as: How do you make AI agents actually useful inside a company?
Context
One phrase kept coming up all evening: context.
Zoom's Huang said AI agents won't become genuinely useful until they understand far more about your company, your colleagues, your meetings, and your work.
"Context is all you need," XD quipped, riffing on the famous AI research paper "Attention is All You Need."
Glean's Vishwanath agreed. He said AI agents often fail because they're connected to too little information — or worse, the wrong information. They confidently produce plausible answers that aren't actually correct. Giving the right context to AI systems at work could now be more important to building smarter models.
That theme cropped up repeatedly.
Ashraf Karim, who leads ServiceNow's internal rollout of its own AI products before customers get them, said the company first used AI to help human support staff before gradually allowing AI agents to handle simpler customer requests themselves. Humans using AI are now delivering even higher customer satisfaction scores than humans working alone because they resolve problems faster and generate more personalized answers.
Biilmann, the CEO of Netlify, argued that writing code is rapidly becoming a commodity. The scarce skills are increasingly domain expertise and software judgment. Companies, he said, may eventually reorganize engineering teams around those strengths rather than around people simply writing code.
Hiring
Hiring sparked one of the liveliest debates of the evening.
Several executives described what one attendee called a "barbell" strategy: hiring very experienced engineers who can question AI-generated work alongside younger graduates who are naturally fluent with AI tools.
Clemm, Figma's engineering VP, warned that engineers in the middle of their careers could face the most pressure as organizations flatten and managers increasingly favor senior hires.
Inworld's Gibbs said startups don't have that luxury. His company is leaning even harder into experienced engineers who can solve the difficult technical problems AI still can't. If AI can already do something in a day, he argued, it probably isn't where your competitive advantage lies.
Optional software
At one point, Tigli, the CTO of MinIO, showed me something that captured another theme of the evening: How AI is changing the software business and making some software unnecessary.
Earlier that day, he'd asked Claude Code to create a presentation. Not in PowerPoint. Not in Google Slides. Claude generated a single HTML file instead. He opened it on his laptop, then AirDropped the same file to his iPhone. It worked perfectly on both devices. No presentation software. No cloud service. Just a file.
This is often how software gets disrupted. Not with a dramatic product launch, but with people quietly discovering a simpler way to get the same job done. If AI can build a presentation from a prompt and package it into a portable HTML file, how much do you really need Microsoft PowerPoint or Google Slides?
Predictions
I ended the dinner with one final question: "What will we laugh about doing manually two years from now?"
Several people predicted status meetings would largely disappear because AI agents would already know what everyone had accomplished. That echoes what OpenAI is already seeing internally: some research teams have stopped holding troubleshooting office hours because researchers increasingly rely on AI instead.
Then Lime CTO Jon Jenkins produced one of the night's biggest eyebrow-raisers.
He suggested software engineers won't be the only people wondering whether AI can do their jobs.
Within two years, perhaps C-suite executives (like those around the table) will be asking themselves the same uncomfortable question.

ai_agent.title: How AI Agents Are Helping Companies Scale Their Marketing
ai_agent.summary_original: Here's how AI agents can help companies scale marketing by combining skills, tools and context into an agentic marketing operating model.
ai_agent.content_original:
How AI Agents Are Helping Companies Scale Their Marketing
Here’s how AI agents can help companies scale marketing by combining skills, tools and context into an agentic marketing operating model.
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
Key Takeaways
- Agentic Marketing shifts AI from helping marketers create content to actually executing full workflows on their behalf.
- The framework boils down to one formula: Skills + Tools + Context = Agency.
- As AI takes on more execution, marketers should move from approving every step (human-in-the-loop) to supervising the system and intervening only on high-risk decisions (human-on-the-loop).
There is a unique opportunity in the market to create “agency” within marketing departments with the power of AI agents. I have been in marketing for more than 25 years, and I could not be more excited to scale marketing with AI. Let me introduce you to “Agentic Marketing”
As a company grows, marketing quickly becomes a collection of specialized functions. Product marketing defines positioning and messaging. Demand generation creates pipeline. Creative teams build assets. Growth marketers reach the right accounts. Social and paid media distribute content. Analytics measures performance. Marketing operations connects the systems. In many industries, legal and compliance also need to review what reaches customers.
Large companies may have hundreds of people across these functions. Startups do not have that luxury. And actually, beyond the top 500 companies, many organizations don’t have that marketing investment as well.
AI agents are beginning to change the equation.
I call this shift Agentic Marketing, a new way of executing marketing where AI agents can reason, use specialized skills, access business context and take actions across marketing workflows.
The most important word is agency; generative AI helped marketers create faster. Agentic AI can increasingly help them execute. For entrepreneurs, that could make sophisticated marketing capabilities available much earlier in the life of a company.
Marketing automation was only the beginning
Marketing has used automation for decades. A prospect downloads an ebook, and an automated workflow sends an email. A lead reaches a certain score, and the system routes it to sales. A customer abandons a shopping cart, and a follow-up campaign starts automatically.
These systems are valuable, but most traditional marketing automation follows predetermined rules: if this happens, do that. Agentic systems can handle a broader objective.
Imagine telling your marketing system, “Launch a campaign for our new product targeting the top 50 financial services accounts.”
There is no single workflow that can answer that request. The system needs to understand the product, identify the right personas, research target accounts, determine the messaging, create campaign assets, check brand requirements, validate claims, select channels, launch approved content and measure performance.
That requires the system to interpret an objective, determine what needs to happen and take authorized actions toward the outcome.
That is where Agentic Marketing begins.
From marketing departments to marketing capabilities
Consider how a traditional marketing organization works. Product marketing develops positioning and go-to-market strategy. Demand generation turns that strategy into campaigns. Creative teams build the assets. Account-based marketing teams personalize programs for high-value customers. Social and paid media teams distribute the content.
Marketing operations connects the systems, analytics evaluates performance and legal reviews claims before they reach customers. Each function contributes a different capability. Agentic Marketing creates an opportunity to represent some of those repeatable capabilities as specialized AI skills.
A Product Marketing Agent might analyze competitors and develop a messaging brief. A Customer Insights Agent could identify recurring customer pain points. An ABM Agent might research a target account and determine which value propositions are most relevant. A Brand Agent could review content against established standards. A Performance Agent could analyze campaign results and recommend changes. An Orchestrator Agent could coordinate the work across all of them.
For startups, this is a meaningful shift. Instead of asking how many people are required to build every marketing function, founders can start asking which capabilities can be turned into repeatable, agent-powered workflows.
The Agentic Marketing Framework
I believe companies can start building an Agentic Marketing operating model around three components: Skills, Tools and Context.
When these work together, they create agency.
1. Build skills
Start with the work your marketing team repeatedly performs.
Maybe product marketing follows a specific process for analyzing competitors. Your content team may use a framework for evaluating whether messaging is focused on customer outcomes. Your social team may have rules for adapting long-form content into short-form posts. Your brand team likely reviews assets against the same standards repeatedly. These processes can become reusable AI skills.
A skill should represent how your company wants a specific job performed. Instead of repeatedly asking an AI model, “Is this good content?” you can create a Content Review Skill that understands what good content means for your organization. The more repeatable the process, the stronger the candidate for a skill.
2. Connect the tools
Skills become far more useful when agents can act. A campaign agent might need access to a CRM. A content agent may need a content management system. An analytics agent needs campaign performance data. A social agent needs access to publishing platforms.
Connecting agents to these systems moves AI beyond answering questions and into executing work. This is also where governance matters. Agents should receive only the permissions required for their role. Some actions can happen automatically. Others should require approval. The goal is controlled autonomy.
3. Provide context
Context may be the most important part of the model.
A generic AI model knows very little about your company. It does not inherently know your positioning, customer personas, approved messaging, competitive landscape, pricing strategy, previous campaigns, brand standards or legal requirements. That context is what allows agents to make better decisions.
There is a major difference between asking, “Create a campaign for CFOs,” and giving an agent access to your product messaging, customer research, previous campaign performance, brand guidelines, customer references and target account data before making the same request. Skills define how work gets done. Tools determine what actions can be taken. Context helps the system understand what to do and why.
Skills + Tools + Context = Agency.
Keep humans in the loop
Marketing directly shapes how customers experience your company, so autonomy needs guardrails. A poorly designed agentic system can distribute inaccurate information, make inappropriate claims or generate enormous amounts of low-quality content very quickly. Nobody needs more AI slop.
As content becomes cheaper to create, the quality bar should rise. That is why I believe marketing leaders should think about moving from human-in-the-loop toward human-on-the-loop systems.
Humans define the objective, establish the context, create the guardrails and determine which decisions agents can make autonomously. They supervise the system and step in when a decision carries greater brand, financial, legal or customer risk. The opportunity is to increase the speed of the marketing engine while preserving accountability and quality.
The opportunity for entrepreneurs

ai_agent.title: Why ‘random acts of AI’ fail — and how to make agentic workflows stick
ai_agent.summary_original: Google’s Official Digital Marketing Publication. Explore how marketers can make agentic workflows stick through AI integration and governance.
ai_agent.content_original:
Over the past couple of years, marketing departments have been scrambling to test every generative AI tool, plug-in, and extension in what feels like an era of “random acts of AI.” But spinning up AI pilots is not the same as engineering agentic workflows. It’s why that, according to McKinsey’s research, while 90% of CMOs are experimenting with gen AI, less than 10% are realizing real value with AI.
To drive value, marketers must shift from tool accumulation to system design. It’s time to account for AI in your workstreams and put building, directing, and managing AI agents in marketers’ job descriptions. That’s the approach we’ve been taking on my team in Google Cloud Marketing. Let me share how we are doing it.
Shift from ‘random acts of AI’ to collective workforce capability
Like many marketing teams, when we started experimenting with generative AI, we focused on personal productivity. It was something we used to draft a quick email, brainstorm a headline, or summarize a report. Our approach was fragmented and bottom up.
If agents reliably automate 80% of routine tasks, team roles must be redesigned, elevating strategic judgment, context, and empathy.
Moving from that individual activation phase to a systemic rewiring of our work required connecting stand-alone capabilities into a cohesive, ecosystem where partners and human talent utilize AI systems directly. We challenged ourselves to redefine our roles. If we automate tasks with AI agents, team roles would need to be redesigned, elevating strategic judgment, context, and empathy.
We created “AI pods,” teams of three to five people from across marketing, agencies, and sales, paired with a “workflow architect.” These pods are tactical and temporary. They are established with a clear goal and dissolve after that objective is achieved. The people building the agents were the front-line marketers who knew the work best and could best build and direct AI agents.
Map taxonomies and agent archetypes
You can’t reengineer a workflow if you don’t actually know what it’s made of. To move from pilots to production, we ran an audit of our team’s process dependencies — a foundational step documenting marketing activity, taxonomy, and architecture.
We established a granular understanding of marketing microtasks and mapped them directly to agent archetypes to assist with things like research, analysis, and content operations. The goal is to optimize and then reimagine legacy workflows and ultimately create entirely new ways of working. By breaking down complex workflows into structured microtasks, we could build specialized agent combinations that integrate seamlessly into our work.
For example, we agentified our integrated marketing campaign workflow. The process begins when a marketing owner defines objectives and uploads key information into a central intelligence layer. Grounded in this data, the AI agent scans calendars and budgets to flag redundancies and find opportunities. The agent then notifies relevant stakeholders and generates three distinct brief options for a human marketer to review, consolidate, and approve.
Once the brief is approved, the agent outlines digital and event requirements, and distributes the approved strategy to our agency and internal partners. As these partners build campaign elements, the agent localizes, translates, and resizes creative assets under close human supervision. Finally, the AI agent performs brand compliance checks before marketing leadership gives the ultimate sign off. Approved assets are added to a central folder where performance is tracked, resources are shared, and impact reports are automatically generated. With AI agents, we’ve accelerated this process 2X to 3X, compressing a weeklong cycle into just two days.
Set clear criteria and reviews for AI agents
AI initiatives often fizzle because they lack formal governance, explicit ownership, and clear goals. Lasting AI impact requires human marketers to manage and review AI agents and their work. For example, a content marketer managing a copywriting agent would bring their personal experiences, product knowledge, and audience context to review AI drafts. The manager is responsible for auditing outputs and fine-tuning prompt instructions.
We developed an AI agent review rubric for managers focused on key criteria.
- Accuracy: Is the agent output correct and pulling from grounded, verified facts?
- Speed: Is execution running smoothly and efficiently without lagging, and keeping up with the pace of the market?
- Brand compliance: Is the output on brand, and within style and specifications guidelines?
- Value: Is the customer benefiting from our improved workflows?
How to lead in the agentic era
As AI reliably automates more and more operational execution, marketing leaders and their teams must pivot to focus on strategic steering, context-setting, and high-empathy leadership. These deeply human capabilities are more valuable than ever in the era of AI agents.
Ultimately, we aren’t building agents; we are building human capabilities. By taking the administrative weight off our marketers’ shoulders, we empower them to do what they do best: steer the system, grow as leaders, and drive high-impact creative ideas forward.

ai_agent.title: We Built an Alternative to Vector RAG for AI Agent Memory
ai_agent.summary_original: What agentic RAG is, how it differs from traditional retrieve-then-generate pipelines, when vector databases still make sense, and how to design document capabilities for agents.
ai_agent.content_original:
Back to blog
Agentic RAG vs vector RAG: two separate choices for document agents
Agentic vs fixed pipelines and vector vs keyword search are separate choices. How to pick for document agents, and when you can skip retrieval entirely.
Updated after feedback on Hacker News. The first version treated "agentic" and "vector" as a single decision. They aren't, and this version is rewritten around that.
Retrieval-augmented generation started as a pipeline. Chunk the documents, embed the chunks, store the vectors, and before each answer pull the nearest passages and hand them to the model. It's easy to describe, which is partly why it's still what most tutorials teach.
Agents changed the shape of that, not what's inside it. Once models were reliable at calling tools, retrieval turned into something the model can do, repeat or skip, and many teams have worked that way for a while. What didn't change on its own is what sits behind the tool call. In a lot of document projects it's still a vector search over chunks, because that's what the tutorial built.
What RAG for AI agents means
It means giving an agent access to information outside its context while it works. In a fixed pipeline that access happens once, up front. In an agentic setup it's a tool the agent calls whenever it decides it needs something.
Fixed pipeline
question → embed → vector search → chunks → model → answer
Agentic
task → agent decides what it needs → calls a search or document tool
     → looks at the result → calls another tool, or acts
Nothing in the second flow says the search tool uses embeddings. It could be a BM25 index, a SQL query or a document API. That's the next section.
Two choices that get mixed up
Any option in the first row combines with any option in the second. An agent can call a BM25 index. A fixed pipeline can run hybrid search. So "agentic RAG vs vector RAG" compares things on different axes, which is why those arguments tend to go in circles. It also means that calling keyword search "not RAG" is wrong: RAG only requires that retrieved text feeds the model, whatever did the retrieving.
Where fixed vector pipelines struggle with documents
Chunking breaks structure. Split an invoice's line-item table across two chunks and a row like "Widget B, 12, 4.50" ends up in a passage with no column headers. Cut a contract clause away from its definitions section and "Term" means whatever the model assumes. Documents aren't made of interchangeable fragments.
Similarity isn't comparison. Embeddings can tell you two passages are about the same thing. They can't tell you that 48,320€ is the right sum of three line items. "Does this invoice match the purchase order" asks for a comparison of specific values, and nearest-neighbor search doesn't compare anything.
One lookup is rarely enough. Finding a contract, then its latest amendment, then the renewal clause, then checking a date against the notice period is several steps, each depending on the last. A fixed chain assumes one retrieval covers it. This is the part the agent loop genuinely fixed.
Vector stores come with upkeep. Ingestion, re-embedding when parsing changes, index updates, deletions, access control, and evaluating whether retrieval is any good. None of it is exotic, but it's work that exists before the product does anything.
None of this makes vector search a bad tool. If someone asks for everything in a company wiki related to data retention, without knowing which words the authors used, embeddings do something keyword search can't. The complaint is about using them as the default for documents where the questions are about exact values.
What agentic retrieval looks like
The agent decides whether it needs to retrieve at all, picks a source, rewrites its query if the first attempt was off, checks whether the result is enough, and either tries again or stops. The tools it gets can be as ordinary as search_documents(), query_document(), compare_documents(), extract_fields(), query_database() and request_human_review().
This is the baseline now, not a frontier. The open question is what those tools do well for documents specifically: tables, versions of the same file, two documents that disagree, evidence that isn't there.
How retrieval for agents evolved
Roughly in this order: retrieve and generate; add reranking; mix vector, keyword and metadata filters in a hybrid setup; then let the agent call retrieval as a tool instead of running it on a fixed path. The last step isn't new anymore. What's still being worked out is the layer under it.
Alternatives to vector-based retrieval
Calling these "alternatives to RAG" is loose, since most of them still hand external context to a model. They differ in how that context gets chosen.
Structured extraction. Turn the document into fields (supplier, total, tax, due date), validate them, and write them to another system. When the workflow depends on known fields, this beats retrieving passages.
Direct document querying. Send the document with the question, no indexing first. Good for one-off uploads and short documents.
Multi-document comparison. Send an invoice, a purchase order and a delivery note together and ask whether they agree. That's checking relationships across files, not searching.
Keyword and hybrid search. BM25 on its own is often enough when people search with the same terms the documents use. Combined with vectors it covers a lot of ground.
SQL, APIs and graphs. Overdue invoices or supplier limits are more precise as a query than as a similarity search. Knowledge graphs capture relationships that similarity doesn't.
Full-document context. For small and medium documents, giving the model a clean, structured version of the whole thing can be more reliable than splitting it.
RAG over documents for agents
"RAG over documents" often just means PDFs in a vector store, which is one implementation. An agent working with documents might need to read a file, extract fields, ask follow-up questions, compare two files, point to where a number came from, notice that a file is missing, and flag what it can't resolve. That's closer to a set of document tools than to an index.
Where Claix fits
Claix is a document API we built for agents. It doesn't use embeddings or chunking, and "no vector database" on its own says very little, so here is what it does.
A file goes through a conversion specific to its format (PDF, Excel and CSV, Word, images, audio, text, HTML, XML) into either markdown or JSON validated against a schema you define. Stored documents can be fetched back as markdown with get-document, or queried with typed questions. You send up to five questions, each tagged with the type you expect (string, int, boolean, timestamp or array), and get typed answers back in the same order.
Documents can be grouped into a knowledge space, and the same questions can be asked across the whole group. There is no retrieval step in that call. The scope is set by recency and size: the 50 most recent live documents, within a shared budget of 200,000 characters. If a document is trimmed to fit, the model is told what it didn't see. With source verification enabled, each answer carries a source, naming the documents by ID and file name and saying which ones were combined to get a number. When the documents don't support an answer, the field comes back as requires_human_revision instead of a guess.
That design has a ceiling, and it's worth saying plainly. It works when the documents that matter for a question are few enough to read directly: one supplier's invoices and contract, an applicant's file, a single case. If you have thousands of documents and the hard part is finding the right five, you need a retrieval step in front, and whether that's embeddings, BM25 or a SQL filter is its own decision. Claix doesn't make that selection for you. It handles what comes after: reading the documents you picked and answering typed questions about them with a source attached.

ai_agent.title: How Microsoft Is Trying to Keep Your AI Agents Contained
ai_agent.summary_original: Microsoft’s Execution Containers give Windows developers a “kill switch” and “YOLO mode” in terms of access for AI agents.
ai_agent.content_original:
If you’ve read even one news story from the AI industry recently, it’s probably been some version of this: An AI agent, or bot, from a major lab got out of its testing environment and found its way onto the internet, hacking real websites. That’s because it’s happened to several major AI companies (including Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic), with hacked sites including the AI platform Hugging Face and sites operated by the US and Australian governments.
To help prevent these kinds of agent-driven cybersecurity breaches, Microsoft is betting on new enterprise software to corral AI agents.
They’re called Microsoft Execution Containers, or MXC, and they live in your developer’s sandbox on Windows. They have two main purposes: to identify and then restrain AI agents. Using these “containers” — which are really just a layer of software applied on top of your existing work — helps you limit what files and network designations your AI agent can access. CEO Satya Nadella said on Wednesday that MXC is now generally available during the company’s Surface Laptop Ultra event.
The idea is that your AI agent will get in less trouble — and cause less damage — if it only has access to specific files and designations on your laptop. Windows developers can choose from three levels of access to grant their AI agents. The recommended level gives your agent access to the internet (essential for many agentic tasks) as well as limited access to areas of your PC, such as your downloads, documents and desktop.
The most restrictive mode is Locked Down, which can serve as a kind of kill switch for access. It restricts your agent’s access to the internet and your files. Unprotected is the complete opposite and gives the AI the most access to your digital ecosystem. You can toggle between them and customize access as needed.
You can also monitor what your agent is doing and how much of your CPU, memory, disk and network you and your AI agent are using. In the example below, the user in the top line is the human logged into Windows. You can see their AI agent (R2-W9 (20)) at work accessing OpenClaw and an Nvidia container.
Safety controls like MXC have been and will continue to be essential for AI labs, particularly as personal AI agents like Meta Muse and OpenAI’s dots become more popular. The rogue agent hacks we’ve seen this summer targeted websites, but it’s easy to hypothesize that, as these agents become more widespread and embedded in our systems, the consequences could easily bleed into the real world.
For Microsoft specifically, which is focused on hard-selling its AI to enterprise customers, it needs to be able to assure a company that its AI won’t wreak havoc on their business. CEO Satya Nadella rightly said that tech companies like Microsoft will have to earn people’s trust to get them to use its agentic AI tools.
“If you look at the first decision we are making, it’s what … authority that I’m giving to the agent on my behalf?” Nadella said on Wednesday. “And that is a decision that will be based on trust and will keep increasing the more autonomous [AI] is.”
But no AI safety program is totally bulletproof. Part of that is the nature of new technology. But debate over whether the AI industry is doing enough to make AI safe has reached a fever pitch recently. AI experts and the general public are rightly concerned that AI labs’ drive to grow fast and break things could lead to disaster for us all.
At the very least, AI leaders seem to understand that safety is key for AI. Or, they’re including it higher up in their sales pitch.
“It’s about trust. It’s about containment. It’s about monitoring,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at the event. “If we can’t get that right, that’s the first part.”

ai_agent.content_original:
Researchers Are Tracking a Chinese AI 'Agent Fleet' (techcrunch.com) 11
			
		 	
				Independent researchers say they've identified a large "fleet" of AI agents apparently running on Tencent infrastructure and making parallel queries against Alibaba's Amap mapping service. TechCrunch reports:  Researchers, however, resisted the term "swarm," noting that there seems to be little coordination between their different queries. "'Agent fleet,' not 'swarm:'" one researcher wrote in the preliminary report, "many parallel agents on the same kind of task, with no sign of communication between them." The agents were discovered by monitoring traffic to the domain-scanning service urlquery, a technique that previously revealed long-running activity by OpenAI agents. AI agents often use urlquery to load websites that they cannot access directly, leaving a record of their activities that can be valuable to researchers.
In this case, the record showed queries to Alibaba's Amap service, seeking directions to different entrances of various public places, including a park, a zoo, and a hospital. The research is ongoing and so few details are available, but the behavior shows how persistent AI agent activity has become on the internet. In the wake of the Hugging Face incident, many researchers are actively monitoring for rogue agent activity on the internet. Much of that activity has been easy to find because agents tend to use the same techniques and make little effort to conceal themselves.

ai_agent.title: Forever Junior: The Skills AI Can't Develop for You
ai_agent.summary_original: AI can write code, but it cannot make you senior. Learn how curiosity, emulation, autonomy, and collaboration help engineers grow in an agentic world.
ai_agent.content_original:
It’s an agentic world.
Software engineering is going through an AI revolution we’re all still trying to understand. For years, we’ve been told software engineers are six months from extinction. Some still believe the job is disappearing. Others say it’s simply changing.
My experience says it’s the latter.
My fear with AI
I’ve seen a real shift in priorities for engineers, but the job itself is very much still needed. At Criteo, engineers are still hired, still valued — and increasingly asked to lean on AI agents to boost productivity as much as possible. But every one of those messages comes with the same addendum: keep a firm hand on the wheel. Use the tool, but don’t stop knowing what you’re doing.
As a Junior fresh out of school, “still learning what I’m doing” isn’t a caveat — it’s the job description. So it’s tempting, and a little dangerous, to let an agent not just do the work, but learn it in my place. It knows much more than I do, after all!
We were taught in school that the way to get better at this job is to just code. Now we’re told not to code directly if we can help it. So — how are we supposed to learn? That’s the extinction I’m actually afraid of: not Software Engineers disappearing, but Seniors disappearing — as we all become forever Juniors, only ever qualified to review one agent’s work with the help of another.
So what was I supposed to do about it?
I started by researching two questions:
- What has AI actually changed in my job description?
- What’s a Senior, concretely?
To answer the former question I just had to listen to discourse online and at work. Many are saying that reviewing code is now more important than producing it. The consensus seems to be that learning coding syntax and languages is obsolete. And of course companies want us to focus on things like token management to optimize costs.
For the latter question, I observed Seniors at work, specifically in my team, and picked up some keys to what Seniorhood meant. On my team, the Seniors are the ones who can defend code they’ve shipped, argue a design choice instead of just having one, tell when an agent is heading the wrong way, know when to delegate and when to just do it themselves — and take the time to teach the rest of us.
With these guidelines, I made a map of where I needed to grow with my first milestone being to get nominated for a promotion by the end of the year. As I follow this map, I hope to reach Seniorhood one day.
The next question was how. Clearly, I needed to develop skills.
I started, like a lot of engineers did, writing a skill.md: instructions and patterns fed to a model so it would behave more like a mentor teaching me about Senior behaviors. It’s useful, sure. But somewhere in that process I noticed the real gap wasn’t in my agent’s behavior — it was in mine. So the focus of this article isn’t really about the skills I wrote. It’s about the ones I had to develop in myself to keep up with the ones I was developing with the agent. The ones that I believe will actually allow me to evolve from Junior to Senior.
Questioning
I started by instructing my agent to ask me Socratic questions to test my understanding of the plan or the code itself. A little pop-quiz at the end of each decision or code change. In practice, the questions were relevant only half of the time and they were mostly useful to prompt me to look closely at the plan or code and talk with the agent to make sure I understood it.
# Understanding checks and delegated work
- After implemented work, prompt understanding—rotate style: e.g. explain in their own words, predict what breaks if X changes, walk through one failure mode, defend a trade-off in one sentence. Gently correct and re-check if needed.
- Subagents or delegated tasks must follow the same rules: no unconfirmed mutations and no unconfirmed mutating verify (subject to the same-task verify rule after approved implementation).Code language: Markdown (markdown)
That’s when I noticed I was building a human skill of my own. One every five-year-old already has mastered as they ask “but why,” on repeat, until someone caves.
Curiosity.
The best trick an LLM has is that it speaks your language back to you — so use it. Ask your agent to explain a decision you don’t follow. Ask it to cite a source when it name-drops something unfamiliar. Ask it to justify a suggestion that just feels off. That last one is the real trick: making an agent explain a flawed solution out loud is often how it catches its own mistake — and how you catch it too.
A Senior can defend code they’ve shipped to production. They can argue their design choices. They can tell when an agent is going the wrong way and redirect. Question your agent enough, and you’re rehearsing exactly that.
Yes — this costs tokens. Fair. But I’ve found it’s more efficient overall to slow down here, because code I actually understand before I ship it works in production far more often. And when it doesn’t, I can fix it myself instead of round-tripping with the agent again. I’d rather use AI a little less often, and get properly curious every time I do, than push code that’s only half-understood and pay for it later.
Reviewing
If you’re coding with an agent as much as possible, you’re going to spend most of your time reviewing its work instead. Reviewing is its own skill — arguably the one you’ll need most to actually reach Seniorhood — especially in this AI landscape. The good news is, you’re already sitting on a training set for it: every comment a Senior has ever left on your code.
Pay attention to the patterns. Constantly getting notes on naming? Your team clearly cares about naming conventions — check every name in your agent’s code twice. Do it enough, and you start to notice the practices that are specific to your industry, your company, even your team. And with that you can practice emulation.
# Similarity to existing code and reusability
For each substantive task:
1. Discover — Search the codebase (and/or ask the user) for the closest existing feature (same kind of entity, resource, table, API surface, etc.).
2. Align — Summarize candidates; ask which analogue is best. If nothing fits, ask the user to confirm the work is net-new.
3. Anchor — State the chosen reference (paths, components, patterns) and keep it for the rest of the thread.
4. Plan and implement (when confirmed) — When outlining or implementing, call out divergences from the reference. If the reference is one-off, ask whether a small shared abstraction could serve both without over-engineering.
5. Information gaps — If the user omitted details the reference implies (fields, ownership, API shape), ask before assuming.Code language: Markdown (markdown)
My team owns a product catalog. Every time I added a new entity type in it, Seniors would say some version of “this looks a lot like this one we already have.” So I started using that existing entity as a template — and when I pushed code for review, I watched reviewers scrutinize every deviation from the template entity. The pattern was unmistakable: justify any deviation, reuse whatever you can. Once I saw it, I could apply it myself, reviewing my agent’s output before a colleague ever had to.
I took it a step further and wrote the pattern into my skill — the markdown-file kind, this time, fed straight to the agent. Now it has the pattern in mind before I even open the review. You can push this further too: point AI at your own git history or team chat and have it surface the reviewing patterns for you.
Funny enough, that’s the two meanings meeting in the middle: I built a skill so I could get better at a skill. The file makes the agent’s first draft look more like my team’s code; reviewing that draft anyway, over and over, is what slowly turns me into a better reviewer. In the end, hopefully, I won’t be a Junior with a good skill file. I’ll be the Senior who wrote the comments that went into it.

ai_agent.title: The Python Coding Stack: 1. What makes an AI agent different from a chatbot?
ai_agent.summary_original: Agents Unpacked • Chapter 1: Tools let a system act, but who chooses what happens next?
ai_agent.content_original:
AI agents are often described as the next step beyond chatbots. But what does that step involve? A chatbot can already search the web, write code, and sometimes run it. Is an agent simply a chatbot with more tools, or is something different happening behind the conversation? That’s where we’ll begin Agents Unpacked, a series of conversations exploring what AI agents are, how they work, and when they’re useful.
You ask an AI to organise a folder of photographs. It might tell you how to do it. Or it might start doing the work. Does that make it an agent? In this first Agents Unpacked conversation, Monty and I use photographs and planning a day out to explore what changes when a model can choose actions, inspect the results, and decide what to do next. Along the way, we separate that flexibility from permission, accuracy, and the ability to know when a job is finished.
Who’s Monty? Monty is my personal AI agent. Read an introduction to this series here: Stephen’s Preface to Agents Unpacked
In conversation • Chapter 1
Monty:
Imagine you give a chatbot this request:
“Here’s a folder of photographs. Organise them into dated folders, flag duplicates, and make a browsable index. Don’t delete anything or change the originals.”
For now, suppose it can only reply with words. It cannot touch the files.
What would you expect it to give you, and what would still be left for you to do?
Stephen:
Hmmm? I guess I need to assume it can read the folder, right? Then, can it read the files’ metadata? Can it actually see and analyse the photos themselves? You said “it cannot touch the files”, so I suppose it can’t really do anything for me, right?
Monty:
You’re right. I left its access unclear. “Cannot touch” was sloppy wording.
Let’s say it can inspect the folder, read dates stored with the photographs, and view the images, but cannot create, move, or change files.
It could then give you something useful: “These photographs belong in these date groups. These two files are identical. This one has no recorded date.” But you’d still have to do the organising.
So the first distinction is describing what should happen versus making it happen. Shall we now give it permission to create organised copies, while leaving the originals alone?
Stephen:
Let’s go ahead, yes.
Monty:
Now it can do the organising, rather than merely recommend it. It can create dated folders and put copies into them, leaving the originals unchanged.
But being able to act isn’t, by itself, what makes something an agent. A simple sorting program can do that too.
Here’s where our synthetic sample gets interesting: one image has no recorded date. The system encounters a gap in the information it needs.
What would you want it to do with that image?
Stephen:
If I was doing that manually, I’d try to look at other photos where the scene is similar, the people are wearing the same clothes, and make an educated guess on the date if I can. But that’s how I as a human would do it.
Monty:
That’s a sensible investigation: look for more evidence before deciding.
A system with suitable image-analysis tools could try something similar. But matching clothes or scenery would support an estimated date, not establish one. It shouldn’t quietly turn a guess into a fact.
And your approach helps us sharpen the distinction: a program could have a preset instruction saying “if the date is missing, compare photographs”. Alternatively, a model could choose that investigation after discovering the missing date.
The outward action might look identical. The difference is who—or what—selects the next step.
Stephen:
I suppose I could ask the system to ask me to confirm each of these edge cases. Although after a while, if I feel it’s doing a good job at estimating, I may want it to go ahead without my input.
Monty:
Yes, you can give it more room to act as your confidence grows. For example: “Ask me about every estimated date” could become “Group those photographs without asking, but keep their dates labelled as estimates.”
That changes how much independence you allow, not whether the system is an agent. An agent can stop and ask you. It doesn’t have to always work unattended.
There are two separate questions here: how does it choose its next action, and which actions may it take without your approval? More permission doesn’t make its guesses more accurate.
Stephen:
Go ahead, I’m curious now.
Monty:
Let’s follow the missing-date photograph one step further.
The model chooses to look for related photographs. The tools return a result: there’s a similar scene, but that photograph has no date either.
Now the model has to choose again: investigate another clue, ask you, or leave the photograph undated. Its next action depends on what it just found.
That’s the useful working picture of an agent: a model chooses an action, gets a result, then uses that result to choose what to do next, within agreed limits.
People use “agent” in different ways, so this is a useful working distinction for our conversation, not a universally agreed definition.
But couldn’t a carefully written program also respond to those results?
Stephen:
A carefully written program would need to take care of every eventuality, I suppose. Whereas an LLM can deal with every situation, with the trade-off that it may make mistakes.
Monty:
Close. But I’d soften both “every” claims.
A fixed program can have a fallback for cases its designer didn’t anticipate: “If none of these rules fits, put the photograph in ‘undated’.” It doesn’t need a separate rule for every possibility.
An LLM can propose a next step for situations that weren’t explicitly anticipated, but that doesn’t mean it can handle every situation successfully. It can misunderstand, lack the right tools, or pursue an unhelpful approach.
So the distinction is following a predefined process versus letting the model choose how to proceed, and not limited software versus unlimited intelligence.
Stephen:
Go ahead.
Monty:
Let’s try the same distinction with a day out.
Imagine a visitor planning a museum day in Oxford. The system checks opening times and walking routes, then puts together an itinerary.
Now suppose one museum is unavailable.
One system follows a preset rule: “Replace it with Museum B.” Another lets the model choose what to investigate next, considering the visitor’s interests, remaining time, and budget.
Both might produce the same revised itinerary. What would you need to know to tell which process was agent-like?
Stephen:
I’d need to know the steps the system took between finding out that the first museum is closed and proposing the second one.
Monty:
Yes. The steps and how they were selected, rather than just the finished itinerary.
Did the system follow a rule written in advance, or did the model choose to search for alternatives, inspect the results, and decide which option to check next?
A record of searches and tool results helps us inspect that process. We don’t need access to the model’s private internal reasoning. But the steps alone may not settle it: a fixed workflow could perform those same searches.
So a convincing result doesn’t, by itself, tell us whether an agent produced it.
Stephen:
Go ahead.
Monty:
There’s another wrinkle: a chatbot and an agent aren’t necessarily different products.
The same chat window might give you advice about organising photographs, or start a process that inspects files, chooses actions, and creates organised copies.
The window hasn’t changed. What happens behind it has.
And the LLM isn’t doing the copying itself. It requests an action. The surrounding software carries it out and returns the result. The model is one part of the agent system, alongside its tools and controls.
So “it looks like a chatbot” doesn’t tell us whether it can act as an agent.
Stephen:
Some chatbots can also perform actions, such as browsing the web or writing a Python program, say. Is that because they’ve been enhanced with some of the features of agents, but not all? Or am I skipping too far ahead

ai_agent.title: 用不着Ctrl+F了！全新AI论文工具，帮你在原文献里海里捞针
ai_agent.summary_original: 一套生成论文初稿的多智能体工作流
ai_agent.content_original:
用不着Ctrl+F了！全新AI论文工具，帮你在原文献里海里捞针
一套生成论文初稿的多智能体工作流
henry 发自 凹非寺
量子位 | 公众号 QbitAI
我真求你们了，论文都多得看不过来了，怎么自动写论文的工具还在往外冒！
最近，GitHub又又又又上新了一个AI论文生成工具——
Open Academic Paper Gen。
先别急着划走！
除了能自动生成一版带参考文献的初稿以外，Open Academic Paper Gen还有个你必须关注的点——
在能获取文献全文的情况下，它会从全文（划重点）中寻找依据，核验论文里的引用观点。
有一说一，这非常实用了。
因为论文写作很多时候，就是从一个研究主题出发，不断梳理观点、寻找证据，再根据文献调整自己的判断。
有了AI之后，论点可以帮你发散，论据也可以帮你检索来源。
但问题在于，有时候观点、论文是真的，可一旦把（AI给的）“观点”放回全文里，结合上下文语境去看，就会发现，作者可能压根不是那个意思。
所以，为了解决这个问题，Open Academic Paper Gen在拿到文献全文之后，会进一步定位相关段落，判断这篇文献到底能不能支撑对应观点。
如果有页码信息，它还会在注释里标出对应的PDF页码，方便人再回去翻查。
也就是说，它不光会查“这篇论文存不存在”，还会查“这话到底是不是它说的”。
一套生成论文初稿的多智能体工作流
总体来看，Open Academic Paper Gen是一套生成论文初稿的多智能体工作流，把从选题到导出的过程，拆成了九个阶段：
确定研究范围、检索文献、清理筛选、分析趋势、寻找切入点、列提纲、写作、核验，最后导出。
和其他AI论文写作工具类似，你给它一个研究主题，比如“物理世界的RSI”。
它就会从这个主题中拆出具体的研究问题，再生成对应的中英文关键词，去OpenAlex、Crossref、Semantic Scholar和arXiv里搜索论文。
搜回来的文献会进一步去重、评分，再由模型筛选相关性。遇到相关性较高的论文，还会顺着它的参考文献，以及后来引用它的研究继续找。
相当于抓住一篇，再顺藤摸瓜补一批，思路其实有点像当年的CONNCTED PAPERS。
（有没有懂的）。
接下来，收集到的文献，会被整理成一张证据表，汇总每篇论文的研究问题、方法、数据、结论以及局限。
有了这些材料，系统再分析研究趋势，提出可能的研究角度、研究空白和假设。
这里还有个挺有意思的环节，叫创新性诊断。
Open Academic Paper Gen会从问题、方法、数据和视角几个维度评估切入点，指出文献池中最接近的已有工作，并给出审稿人可能提出的质疑。
（这相当于是在你觉得自己做出ResNet时，AI先帮你看看别人是不是做过）
具体的，这些判断会围绕本次检索到的文献展开，不过，文献池里没找到，不代表全世界没人做过～
最后，研究角度确定后，系统继续生成提纲、分章节起草。
初稿写完，再进入引用核验和模拟审稿，最后可以导出 Markdown 或 LaTeX，以及 RIS、BibTeX 等参考文献格式。
在具体的运行方式上，默认模式下Open Academic Paper Gen会在主要阶段停下来，等你审查、编辑、确认后再往下走。
如果想测试一下AI研究的能力，也可以让它自动跑完，选择全自动模式。
最后，准备开跑的朋友还得注意一下模型配置：
目前项目支持OpenAI和智谱GLM，但论点核验、无引用陈述检查和模拟审稿这几个环节，仍然需要 OpenAI API Key。
引用怎么查到句子里？
老实说，自动搜文献、写初稿，再让AI审一遍稿，已经是不少论文写作项目的常见组合。
其中一些还加入了引用核验和人工确认，尽量减少模型瞎编。
Open Academic Paper Gen在这套流程里，进一步细化了引用的检查和修改。
毕竟，给一篇初稿配上参考文献是一回事，证明这些参考文献真的能支撑正文，又是另一回事。
具体来说，它把核验拆成了三道检查。
第一道，检查引用能不能在文献池里找到。
写作时，每个引用标记都要对应已经收集到的一篇论文。
如果模型临时编出一个不存在的引用标识，系统就会把它标出来，方便定位和修改。
第二道，核对这篇文献的身份。
有DOI的论文，会先与Crossref的记录核对；查不到时，再去doi.org确认。
标题、作者、年份等信息对不上，会触发相应警告。
第三道，检查原文到底支不支持这句话。
到了这里，检查才真正从“文献信息”，进入“文献内容”。
拿到全文后，系统会从中找出与引用论点最匹配的段落，连同论文开头一起交给模型，判断原文能不能支撑正文里的说法。
拿不到全文，则使用摘要或节选。存在页码数据时，警告还可以标出对应的PDF页码，方便人回去翻查。
当然了，模型没找到足够证据，不等于已经证明这句话是错的。
按照Open Academic Paper Gen的处理方式，证据不足时可以标为“无法判断”。
文本太少、根本没法核对的文献，则会标为“未核验”，而不是直接算通过。
所以，整体看下来，比起“一键写完论文”，Open Academic Paper Gen把文献整理、证据定位和引用自查串起来的思路的确很灵性。
尤其是面对 AI 写出来的观点和论据，总觉得“好像有道理，但又不敢直接信”的时候，能把对应原文找出来，至少多了一个回去核实的抓手。
By the way，这个项目来自个人开发者猫叔。除了Open Academic Paper Gen，他此前还发布过AI编剧、AI研究等多个项目。

ai_agent.title: 富士通では「Copilot」10万ライセンスの利用率が“9割超え”　「導入したけど使われない」をどう防いだ？
ai_agent.summary_original: 全社にAIを導入しても、実際に使われなければ効果は生まれない。「Microsoft 365 Copilot」を社内導入した富士通は、どのようにしてAI活用を全社に定着させ、日常業務の変革につなげたのか。
ai_agent.content_original:
全社にAIを導入しても、実際に使われなければ効果は生まれない。「Microsoft 365 Copilot」を社内導入した富士通は、どのようにしてAI活用を全社に定着させ、日常業務の変革につなげたのか。
この記事は会員限定です。会員登録（無料）すると全てご覧いただけます。
2026年5月に発表した「中長期経営ビジョン2035」で、データとAIを事業成長の中核に据えた富士通。自社が最初のユーザーとなってAI主導の経営を実践し、その知見で顧客の変革を先導する「Customer Zero」（カスタマーゼロ）戦略を掲げる。
課題は、導入したAIの活用を、国内外の全従業員に浸透させることだった。一部の従業員だけがAIを使っても活用シーンが限られ、効果を最大化できないと判断したからだ。全従業員が日常的にAIを使う状態にして、個人の生産性向上にとどまらない業務プロセスの変革につなげる必要があると、富士通は考えていた。
こうした中、富士通は全社でのAI利用を促す仕組みを整えつつ、Microsoftの生成AIアシスタント「Microsoft 365 Copilot」の全社導入を進めた。その結果、利用率を高い状態で維持し、業務効率化といった具体的な成果も現れているという。どのように全社への導入と活用を進めたのか。
富士通は2025年7月、全社の各部門を対象にMicrosoft 365 Copilotを7500ライセンス導入し、集中トライアルを実施した。その結果を踏まえて、2026年1月に3万ライセンス規模に拡大。同年4月には、ほぼ全従業員向けの約10万ライセンスを本格導入した。
全社展開では「フジトラ」（Fujitsu Transformation）で築いた推進体制を活用した。フジトラは、経営層から現場従業員まで全従業員が参加する社内DX（デジタルトランスフォーメーション）活動だ。
全社でのAI実践を進める部門横断の活動「全社AI実践イニシアティブ」も立ち上げた。トライアル中にはハンズオンセミナーやトレーニング動画を用意し、習熟度に応じてMicrosoft 365 Copilotの使い方を学べるようにした。
個人利用にとどまらないAI活用を促すために、業務システムの改善に関する「AI & DDM Award」（DDM：データドリブン経営）や、AIエージェントの活用に関する「鉄板エージェント コンテスト」といった、優れた取り組みを表彰する社内コンテストを定期的に開催してきた。
富士通がMicrosoft 365 Copilotを選んだのは、「Microsoft Teams」「Microsoft Outlook」など、社内で使ってきたMicrosoftツールでそのまま使えるAIツールであり、日常業務で活用しやすいと判断したからだ。7500ライセンスという大規模なトライアルも、議事録や資料の作成などさまざまな業務シーンで使うことで、早期に効果を最大化する狙いがあった。
導入から2カ月後の2026年6月の時点でも、Microsoft 365 Copilotの利用率は全社で90％以上を維持していた。社内サービスデスク業務では、従業員からの問い合わせに対して、AIエージェントが一次対処や問い合わせ内容の精査を担うことで、年間約30万件の問い合わせプロセスのうち、約75％を自動化できたという。
AIによる自動化で、担当者はより付加価値の高い業務に取り組めるようになった。AIエージェントの回答の基になるFAQ（よくある質問とその答え）や手順書などのナレッジの内容改善や、AIエージェントの回答精度の向上などだ。
富士通はMicrosoft 365 Copilotを起点に、業務特化AIエージェントや業務システムを組み合わせて利用できる「マルチエージェントシステム」の実現を目指す。日本マイクロソフトは2026年9月4日、本事例を公開した。

ai_agent.title: タイムズ、デジタル庁、不正アクセス続出の“魔の9月”　一連の背景にはAIの悪用？
ai_agent.summary_original: 2026年9月、不正アクセス被害の公表が相次ぎました。その理由を説明できる仮説が、AIエージェントによる攻撃の高速化です。「魔の9月」は、AIを悪用したサイバー攻撃が本格化する序章なのでしょうか。
ai_agent.content_original:
2026年9月、不正アクセス被害の公表が相次ぎました。その理由を説明できる仮説が、AIエージェントによる攻撃の高速化です。「魔の9月」は、AIを悪用したサイバー攻撃が本格化する序章なのでしょうか。
この記事は会員限定です。会員登録（無料）すると全てご覧いただけます。
2026年9月は、不正アクセスに関するニュースが異様なほど目に付く1カ月でした。
画像共有サービス「Gyazo」では第三者による不正アクセスによってユーザー情報や画像のメタデータが流出し、美容医療プラットフォーム「Unni」（カンナムオンニ）でも一部APIへの不正アクセスによる個人情報漏えいが発生しました。日本郵便は国際郵便物の「調査請求Web受付サービス」への不正アクセスの可能性を公表。セイコーマートでは、セイコーマートクラブ会員約57万人分の情報が不正アクセスによって漏えいした可能性があることが発表されています。
他にも国内で多数のサイバー攻撃や不正アクセスが公表され、まさに「魔の9月」とも言える状況でした。
その中でもインパクトが大きかったのが、タイムズモビリティ、さくらインターネット、デジタル庁への不正アクセスです。タイムズカーでは約660万件のアカウント情報の流出が確認され、さくらインターネットとデジタル庁では、それぞれ136万563アカウント、約24.6万件の情報が漏えいした可能性があります。
なぜ、これほど立て続けに被害が表面化したのでしょうか。本稿では上記3件の内容を整理した上で、AIエージェントが攻撃者に実戦投入され始めている現状を確認します。その延長線上に、今回の被害続出をどう位置付けられるのかを考えます。
2026年9月に明らかになった3つの事案は、対象となった情報や侵入経路、被害の期間がそれぞれ異なります。一方で、「侵入を完全に防ぐ難しさ」と「侵入後の被害拡大をいかに抑えるか」という、現在のセキュリティ対策の課題も浮かび上がりました。
カーシェアリングサービス「タイムズカー」を運営するタイムズモビリティは2026年9月28日、Webシステムへの不正アクセスによって、退会者や入会未完了者を含む約660万件のアカウント情報を第三者に取得されたと発表しました。
漏えいした情報には氏名や住所、生年月日、電話番号、メールアドレス、パスワードなどに加え、運転免許情報や運転免許証画像などの本人確認書類情報も含まれています。パスワードは復元できない形式で保存されており、クレジットカード情報は流出していないことが確認されています。同社は2026年9月29日、運転免許証画像などの本人確認書類が漏えいしたアカウント数は、約160万件だったと公表しました。
不正アクセスを検知したのは2026年9月25日9時7分。翌26日7時25分までに侵入経路や攻撃元との通信を遮断しました。
特徴的なのは、現在の利用者だけでなく、退会済みの利用者や入会手続きが完了しなかった人の情報まで対象になったことです。サイバー攻撃への備えを考える上では、「現在必要なデータをどう守るか」だけでなく、「そもそもどこまで過去のデータを保持する必要があるのか」というデータ管理の問題も無視できません。
さくらインターネットが2026年9月10日に公表した調査結果によると、販売管理システムに保存されていた会員情報などについて、最大136万563アカウントが第三者に閲覧・取得された可能性があります。ただし、実際に持ち出された明確な事実や二次被害は、現時点で確認されていません。
発端は2026年8月9日、「さくらのレンタルサーバ」のメンテナンス用サーバで検知された異常でした。調査の結果、一部サーバへの不正アクセスとマルウェアの設置に加え、販売管理システムのデータベースへの不正アクセスも判明しています。販売管理システムへの不正アクセスは、2023年4月から2026年3月までの間に起きていました。
レンタルサーバ側で影響の可能性があるのは951アカウントです。2026年8月17日時点の583アカウントから、追加調査で368アカウントが加わりました。
注目すべきは、一部のレンタルサーバとVPS（仮想専用サーバ）の初期パスワードが、ハッシュ化されずに保存されていたことです。初期値から変更済みのパスワードは保存されておらず、変更済みであれば今回の情報で不正ログインされるリスクはないとされています。一方で、初期パスワードを使い続けている利用者には、変更が呼び掛けられました。
もう一つの課題がログです。さくらインターネットでは、2025年7月以降とみられる不審な活動の痕跡も確認しましたが、時間の経過に伴う記録上の制約などから、今回の事案との同一性や侵入経路、顧客情報への影響を客観的に確定できませんでした。
再発防止策として、同社ではEDR（Endpoint Detection and Response）の適用範囲拡大や管理者権限とアクセス権限の総点検、ログの取得、保管、分析体制の強化などを挙げています。
デジタル庁は2026年9月11日、同庁が運用する共通システム「ガバメントソリューションサービス」（GSS）への不正アクセスにより、約24万6000件の個人情報が漏えいした可能性があると発表しました。
GSSは、各府省庁の業務用PCやネットワーク、セキュリティなどを共通化する政府の業務基盤で、ゼロトラストネットワークアーキテクチャの考え方も取り入れています。対象は各府省庁の職員や業務に携わった事業者などで、一般の国民の情報は含まれていません。
異常を最初に検知したのは2026年6月25日です。第三者が保守運用担当者のアカウントを使い、サーバ上の大量のファイルにアクセスしていました。同年7月9日には、ネットワーク接続機器、つまりVPN（仮想プライベートネットワーク）機器の脆弱（ぜいじゃく）性を突いて侵入されたことが判明しています。
内訳は、氏名が約23.6万件、メールアドレスが約23.1万件、電話番号が約9.4万件などです。マイナンバーや金融機関の口座情報、年金番号は含まれていないことが確認されています。
保守運用担当者の認証情報がどう攻撃者の手に渡ったのかは、現時点で明らかになっていません。ゼロトラストの考え方を取り入れていても、入口となる機器に脆弱性が残っていれば侵入を許してしまう。そのことを示した事例と言えるでしょう。
これら3件について、公表された情報の範囲ではAIの関与は示されていません。しかし2026年9月には、AIエージェントを使った攻撃の実態や、AIを使った攻撃手法の発見が相次いで報じられています。
Palo Alto Networksの脅威インテリジェンスチーム「Unit 42」は2026年9月2日（現地時間）、AI支援型の侵入事案を公表しました。人間の攻撃者が最先端のAIモデルと攻撃用のエージェント型AIフレームワークを使い、侵入後の偵察や認証情報の探索、権限取得、クラウド環境への侵入などを自動化していたとのことです。
攻撃に要した時間は10時間未満で、人間のオペレーターだけなら約2週間を要する規模だったといいます。50以上の「MITRE ATT&CK」の手法が確認されました。
しかも攻撃者は、AIに万能な「ハッキング能力」を与えたわけではありません。公開Webサービスを入り口に内部のマイクロサービスを調べ、コード保管庫からトークンやサービス用パスワードを探し、取得した認証情報からさらに権限を拡大するという個々の手法は、これまでも攻撃者が使ってきたものです。
違うのは、それらをAIエージェントが高速かつ並列に実行し、「観測→判断→実行→再計画」のループを短時間で繰り返した点です。攻撃者は目的を設定し、重要な判断は人間が行いつつ、途中の作業をAIに委ねることが可能になっています。
従来なら攻撃者が手作業で調査し、試行錯誤している間に検知できた活動が、自動化によって短時間で完了する可能性があります。侵入されてから対応するまでの猶予は、今や急速に縮まろうとしています。
AIは既存の攻撃を高速化するだけではありません。これまで見過ごされてきた攻撃経路を発見する能力も高まりつつあります。
セキュリティ研究チームのHacktron AIは、「HEIF Heist」と名付けた手法を公開しました。細工したHEIF（「iPhone」などで採用されている画像ファイルフォーマット）画像をOpenAIの公開サポートフォーラムに投稿し、画像デコーダーの欠陥からリモートコード実行（RCE）に至ったといいます。
その後、シングルサインオン（SSO）の別の欠陥も経由し、OpenAIの社内用の「GitHub」リポジトリでプルリクエスト（PR）を作成できたということです。
この過程で、Anthropicの「Opus 4.8」が脆弱性の発見を、「Opus 5」がそれを実行可能なエクスプロイト（攻撃コード）にする工程を担ったとされています。同チームは、AIエージェントとフロンティアモデルの活用で、初期調査からRCEまでを約1〜3日に短縮できたと報告しています。
問題となったのは、フォーラム用OSS（オープンソースソフトウェア）「Discourse」に使われている画像処理ライブラリ「libheif」の古いバージョンでした。上流では既に修正されていたものの、セキュリティ修正として明確に扱われていなかったため、利用者側が緊急性を認識しにくかったということです。
同研究チームは、「Slack」やMeta Platformsの主要製品、「Next.js」のAVIF画像最適化機能、「GitHub Enterprise」などでも、RCEや情報流出につながる事例を挙げています。自社で直接導入していないライブラリが依存関係の奥に潜み、攻撃の足掛かりになり得るということです。
この事例は研究目的であり、実際の攻撃ではありません。それでも、AIが脆弱性の発見から悪用までの時間を大きく縮めることを示しています。同じことを攻撃者がすれば、「パッチ適用までの猶予」は今より短くなるでしょう。
では、2026年9月に不正アクセスが相次いだのは、AIエージェントが本格的に悪用され始めたからなのでしょうか。
現時点では、そこまで断定する材料はありません。タイムズカーやさくらインターネット、GSSなどの事案について、攻撃者がAIエージェントを利用したとの情報は公表されていません。
ただし、Unit 42やHacktron AIの報告からは、AIによってサイバー攻撃の「経済性」が変わり始めていることがうかがえます。
攻撃対象を調べ、脆弱性を探し、認証情報を探索し、次の侵入先を判断するという一連の作業をAIが支援・自動化すれば、1人の攻撃者が同じ時間で試せる対象や手法は増えます。これまで時間や人手の制約から攻撃対象にならなかったシステムも狙いやすくなる可能性があります。
そう考えれば、「魔の9月」はAIエージェント悪用時代の序章だったのではないかという仮説は、今後検証すべき論点になりそうです。
では、防御側も全く新しい対策を始めなければならないのでしょうか。少なくとも今回の事例を見る限り、まず必要なのは基本的な対策の徹底です。
GSSではVPNの脆弱性が侵入口になりました。さくらインターネットの事案では、認証情報の管理やログ保存、EDRによる検知の重要性が改めて浮き彫りになりました。AIエージェントを使った攻撃でも、公開API、コードに埋め込まれたトークン、過大な権限など、従来指摘されてきた弱点が悪用されています。
つまり、AIが攻撃を劇的に高速化しても、攻撃者が利用する「穴」まで全く新しくなるとは限りません。まずは、侵入のきっかけを減らすため、これまでと同様に、以下のような基本的な対策を徹底する必要があります。
一方、全ての侵入を防ぐことは困難です。そのため、侵入された後に被害を広げないための備えも欠かせません。
2026年9月の被害続出がAI悪用の序章かどうかは、今後の動向を見なければ分かりません。ただ、入口を閉じ、侵入後の不審な活動を素早く検知して追跡できる状態を整えておくことは、幅広い攻撃に対して被害を抑えるため備えです。
AIによって攻撃速度が上がるほど、こうした基本対策を「いつかやる」のではなく、「攻撃される前に終えておく」ことの意味は大きくなります。

ai_agent.title: 社内9部門、62体のエージェントをどう運用？　「AI社員」が働く企業の実例
ai_agent.summary_original: AIエージェントが実際に企業の業務を担うようになると、仕事はどのように回るのか。AIに何を任せ、人間は何を担うのか。生成AIの研修やコンサルティング、開発を手掛けるUravationが公開した「AI社員」62体の働き方から、その一例を見てみよう。
ai_agent.content_original:
AIエージェントが実際に企業の業務を担うようになると、仕事はどのように回るのか。AIに何を任せ、人間は何を担うのか。生成AIの研修やコンサルティング、開発を手掛けるUravationが公開した「AI社員」62体の働き方から、その一例を見てみよう。
この記事は会員限定です。会員登録（無料）すると全てご覧いただけます。
企業でAIエージェントが日常的に稼働するようになったとき、業務はどのように回るのか。どの仕事をAIに任せ、どこで人間が関与するのか。多数のAIエージェントを使う場合、それらをどう組織し、管理するのかも課題になる。
生成AIの研修やコンサルティング、開発を手掛けるUravationがその一例を示している。同社は2026年9月10日、社内で稼働する62体のAIエージェントについて、その仕事内容や組織図、一日の動き、人間との役割分担などを公開した。
同社の“AI社員”は、メールの仕分けや会議の準備、営業先の調査、経理処理、Webサイトの監視、システム開発、記事作成など多岐にわたる業務を担う。AI社員の62体は、AIマネジャー9体と、9部門に所属する53体。常時稼働する自動ジョブは250本以上に及ぶという。AIがどのように業務を進め、どこで人間が関与するのか。
同社が公開した内容を基に見てみよう。
組織は、「代表」「人間チーム」「AIマネジャー9体」「9つのAI部門」「53体のAI社員」という5階層で構成されている。人間チームが業務設計、承認、品質判断を担い、AIマネジャーが各部門を取りまとめる。AI社員は全て「Claude Code」で構築されている。
AI社員が所属するのは、「社内窓口・秘書」「広報・マーケティング」「メディア運営」「営業サポート」「経理・総務」「サイト監視・品質チェック」「開発」「経営企画」「人事・研修」の9部門だ。
担当する仕事は幅広い。例えば、社内窓口・秘書部門ではAIが24時間チャットに常駐する他、会議の準備やメールの仕分け、議事録の作成などを担う。営業サポート部門では、商談相手の下調べや案内文、お礼メールの作成、経理・総務部門では請求書や領収書の整理、制度改定の確認などを担当する。
開発部門にも5体を配置し、実装やコードレビュー、セキュリティチェック、テストなどを分担する。サイト監視・品質チェック部門では、Webサイトの死活や記事の鮮度などに加え、監視を担当するAI自体が正常に動いているかどうかも確認する。
AI社員はそれぞれ決められた周期で業務を実行する。例えば、タスクの進捗（しんちょく）を管理するAIは60秒ごと、会議の準備をするAIは5分ごと、メールを仕分けするAIは30分ごとに動く。タスクは「作業中」「レビュー待ち」「人間待ち」といった状態に分けて管理するなど、複数のAIが継続的に動くことを前提に運用している。
公開ページでは、62体それぞれについて担当業務や一日の仕事、成果物のサンプルも掲載している。
AI社員の一日の動きも紹介されている。
午前4時43分にバックアップ係が動き始め、主要システム一式を別拠点に退避させ、7世代分を保持する。午前7時台になると、Webサイト18ページを確認する「ロゴ番人」、その日に商談する相手を調べるリサーチ係、記事ネタの残量を確認する在庫番人が仕事を始める。
午前8時台には、日報係が運営レポートを投稿し、制度ウォッチャーが助成金などの制度改定を前日との差分から確認する。さらに「監視の監視」を担当するAIが、自動ジョブ約140本が正常に動いているかどうかを点検する。
午前9時台に入ると、経理ミラー係が請求書や領収書を整理し、SDR（インサイドセールス）係が営業先への案内文を作成する。メディア運営を担当する出稿係も各メディアへの記事公開を進める。一方、相談窓口を担当する2体は24時間チャットに常駐し、問い合わせを受け付けるAIは問い合わせが入ると数秒で反応するという。
人間が仕事を始める頃には必要な報告や準備がそろい、午前中に一連の実務が進む流れになっている。
Uravationは、AI社員を増やしても事故を起こさないために4つのルールを定めている。
同社は「AIに業務を任せる」と言葉で説明するより、自社で実際に何体のAIが、どの業務を、どの順番で、どこまで人間の承認を挟んで動かしているかを見てもらう方が早いと考え、社内の運用実態を1ページにまとめたという。なお掲載の数値は2026年8月時点の実測に基づく。
